items.title: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?
items.abstract: This paper introduces AgentSSL, a novel approach that frames Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) as a program search problem for machine learning agents. The core contribution is demonstrating that agents can effectively leverage unlabeled data by synthesizing and adapting existing SSL techniques, even with limited supervision. This method shows promise in automating pipeline design for new domains where labeled data is scarce, outperforming human-engineered baselines in many scenarios.

items.title: SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models
items.abstract: SALA's core method is to align latent actions in embodied foundation models by using language descriptions of unpaired human and robot video clips to estimate semantic similarities. This approach overcomes the limitation of existing latent action models that primarily rely on visual reconstruction, which can lead to misaligned action representations. SALA's contribution is enabling dual-axis scaling of these models by effectively bridging the semantic gap between human and robot actions without needing paired data.
items.figure_caption: Overview of SALA. Left: unpaired human and robot videos are related only through language descriptions of their atomic actions. Middle: supervising a latent action tokenizer with these relations organizes latent actions by action semantics rather than by scene. Right: through the aligned latent actions, human videos supervise the same action expert that controls the robot: more human-video pre-training lowers the robot’s action prediction error without additional robot data, and more task-specific human video in post-training raises the real-world success rate.

items.title: Scalable Conversational Assessment: Chat-Based Exams with a Two-Agent LLM Pipeline
items.abstract: This paper introduces a scalable, chat-based system for conversational assessments that mimics oral exams. It employs a two-agent Large Language Model (LLM) pipeline: an interviewer interacts with the student, while a hidden evaluator guides the interview and tracks progress against a rubric. This architecture aims to preserve the interactive and reasoning-focused nature of oral exams while overcoming scalability limitations.

items.title: Human or Synthetic? What a Fixed Budget Buys for Post-Training
items.abstract: This paper investigates the cost-effectiveness of human versus synthetic preference data for post-training large language models. By comparing performance under a fixed budget, they demonstrate that synthetic data is significantly more cost-efficient, achieving strong results at much lower costs than human data. The study highlights that synthetic data often outperforms human data, especially for tasks like summarization, even at substantial budget differences.

items.title: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents
items.abstract: This paper investigates the multifaceted roles of decision models in long-horizon agents, moving beyond their traditional use as "actors." The core method compares decision models and LLMs as actors, judges, and teachers across ALFWorld and WebShop environments. The key contribution is demonstrating that models performing poorly as actors can still be effective teachers, and that judging actions based on their contribution to subgoals, rather than overall success, is crucial for effective learning.
items.figure_caption: One decision model queried in three ways, on the task of putting a heated mug on a table. Actor : choosing the next action. Judge : scoring an action of a recorded trajectory under two contexts (Prefix, Hindsight) and two questions (Value, Progress). Teacher : scoring the actions of policy rollouts, with the centered scores added to the GRPO outcome advantage. The middle row lists the six models we evaluate.

items.title: AI for Biologists: The Knowledge Boundaries of Foundation Models in the Age of Agentic Systems
items.abstract: This paper reviews how foundation models are transforming biological research. It proposes that five key design elements define a model's "knowledge boundary," indicating the scope of reliable outputs. Understanding these boundaries is crucial for researchers and AI agents to effectively and trustworthily utilize these powerful tools.

items.title: AURA 2.0: From User-Driven Responses to Model-Initiated Conversations in Streaming Video
items.abstract: AURA 2.0 introduces Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC) to enable AI assistants to proactively engage users by identifying and discussing relevant events in streaming video. It also incorporates Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) for context-aware tool use and Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) for precise object referencing in both user inputs and model outputs. This moves beyond reactive AI to a more dynamic and contextually aware conversational experience.

items.title: Ballad: Bandit-Based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery
items.abstract: This paper introduces Ballad, a bandit-based system for adaptively routing calls to different Large Language Models (LLMs) during automated heuristic discovery. It challenges the assumption that larger, more expensive LLMs are always better, finding their performance inconsistent. Ballad addresses the non-stationary and entangled reward signals inherent in this process to optimize LLM selection for discovering better heuristics.

items.title: CapLite: Prompt-Injection Defense for Small Language Model Agents without Model-Written Security Artifacts
items.abstract: This paper introduces CapLite, a novel prompt-injection defense for small language model (SLM) agents. Unlike prior methods that rely on the SLM to generate its own security artifacts, CapLite derives its policy from tool schemas and enforces write integrity by committing write calls before tool results are read and only allowing writes where all critical arguments originate from the user's request. This approach effectively prevents prompt injection attacks from manipulating agent actions.

items.title: Compiling Known Rules into Compact Neural Agents: Weight-Space Programming on Unseen Games
items.abstract: This paper introduces Weight-Space Programming (WSP), a method that uses language models to directly generate neural network weights, bypassing traditional training. The core contribution is demonstrating that known game mechanics can be compiled into compact neural agents that generalize to unseen game variations. The research shows that WSP can achieve high performance, even outperforming traditional NumPy players under similar computational constraints.
items.figure_caption: Left: setup. A writer receives a game’s mechanics-only source and returns weights for the fixed actor, a network of its own design, or a Python player, one-shot (1) or with feedback (2). Learned baselines train the fixed actor on the support levels. Right: one state of the public game ls20 ( ARC Prize Foundation, 2026 ) as published and under a template we constructed for this figure. The board and HUD are turned, player, collectibles, walls and the key frame are drawn in other styles, and colours are permuted, which changes 91% of the cells while the mechanics stay the same. The private templates vary geometry, object and HUD style and palette in this way.

items.title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
items.abstract: CoReMem is a framework for coding agents that optimizes memory usage for successive tasks. It achieves this by valuing memory segments based on their predicted usefulness for future, unknown tasks, while also accounting for the costs of storing and accessing this memory. This allows the agent to build a compact, efficient memory and adapt its behavior to leverage it effectively.

items.title: Designing Institutions for Autonomous AI
items.abstract: This paper argues that designing effective "institutions" governing AI interactions is crucial for their collective capabilities and alignment, moving beyond a sole focus on individual AI models. Drawing on established social science theories, it proposes seven principles for creating AI institutions that foster cooperation, reliable judgment, and human accountability. The core contribution is establishing institutional design as a vital, distinct area of AI research.
items.figure_caption: Institutional design as an experimental research programme. Autonomous agents operating under different institutional rules may develop different collective capabilities and patterns of alignment, even when their individual capabilities remain unchanged. Illustrated here for machine science, the same population of research agents is placed under publishing rules imported from human science or under machine-native institutional rules, producing different scientific records. Alternative institutional arrangements can then be compared using matched populations of agents. The outcome measures shown concern collective capability; collective alignment, including adherence to human-defined purposes, institutional constraints and accountability requirements, must be evaluated alongside them. Experimental comparisons can inform the subsequent revision of institutional rules.

items.title: Discovering Effective Agent Memory Designs through Program Evolution
items.abstract: This paper introduces MAPE, a program evolution framework that automatically discovers effective agent memory designs. MAPE iteratively diagnoses and proposes memory program improvements, leading to significant accuracy gains and cost reductions compared to manual designs. The research identifies two key design patterns: retaining raw conversations for evidence and composing retrieved evidence based on query intent, which are shown to improve performance when transplanted into existing memory systems.
items.figure_caption: Overview of MAPE ’s program evolution framework. Candidate programs are proposed using archived designs and diagnostic feedback, checked for execution errors, and evaluated on the search set. Their implementations, results, and diagnoses are retained to guide subsequent proposals. Evolution follows either an accuracy-only objective ( MAPE-A ) or joint accuracy–cost objectives ( MAPE-P ). Shortlisted programs undergo held-out evaluation for final selection.

items.title: Reasoning Supervision and Capability Retention in LoRA Domain Adaptation
items.abstract: This paper investigates LoRA domain adaptation for financial tasks, aiming to improve performance without sacrificing generalization. The core method involves comparing three LoRA training regimes: response-only, single-adapter reasoning (including teacher model traces), and dual-adapter composite training. The contribution is demonstrating that response-only LoRA effectively boosts in-domain performance, particularly calibration and accuracy, while largely preserving the model's general capabilities.

items.title: Skill Adapter: Personalized Modification and Online Routing of General-Purpose Skills
items.abstract: This paper introduces Skill Adapter, a method for personalizing and dynamically routing general-purpose skills for LLM agents. It achieves this by learning local adjustments from user feedback and storing them as "Adapters" linked to core skills. A routing agent then selects the most relevant skills and Adapters based on the current task context, enabling efficient and personalized skill utilization.
items.figure_caption: The influence of user requirements on skill selection and composition. In contract translation, layout-preservation requirements affect document extraction and make layout reconstruction part of the subsequent workflow. Task descriptions and user feedback jointly inform skill adjustments and the selection of execution procedures.

items.title: The Value of Thinking: Learning When to Reason in Hybrid Decision Models
items.abstract: This paper introduces a "zero-or-$T$ thinking" paradigm for hybrid decision models. Instead of deciding how much to reason, a model either answers directly (zero thinking) or performs full autoregressive reasoning ($T$ tokens). A self-routing block estimates the "value of thinking" and triggers full reasoning only when its expected utility exceeds a cost threshold, optimizing for efficiency in agentic tasks.
items.figure_caption: HDM’s zero-or- T T thinking on two JevBench questions. LEFT, a case where the fast mode is sufficient: the predicted value of thinking is below \( \lambda \) , the block answers at no token, and running both modes afterwards confirms the slow mode would not have changed the answer. RIGHT, a case that should go to the slow mode: the predicted value is above \( \lambda \) , routing to the slow mode, and running both modes afterwards confirms the fast answer would have been wrong. Appendix G gives both thinking blocks in full.

items.title: AnalogLayoutWorld: An Open Benchmark for Agentic Analog Layout Design
items.abstract: This paper introduces **AnalogLayoutWorld**, an open benchmark designed to evaluate the capabilities of AI agents in analog circuit layout design. The benchmark provides a realistic environment with expert-reviewed tasks, integrated design tools, and comprehensive verification, addressing the challenges of long-horizon engineering tasks with physical constraints. Its core contribution is establishing a standardized platform for developing and assessing agents in this complex domain, revealing current agent performance and highlighting areas for improvement.
items.figure_caption: Agentic analog layout design process. (a) A fixed netlist, specifications, and process design kit define the task. (b) The agent constructs and refines layouts using layout tools and verification feedback. (c) Integration, fabrication, and silicon characterization provide physical validation.

items.title: Auditing AI peer reviewers: a benchmark on real scientific papers
items.abstract: This paper introduces a benchmark for evaluating AI peer reviewers by injecting specific, localized errors into real scientific papers. The benchmark measures reviewers' ability to detect these errors across different types and severities, alongside their false-positive rates. The authors also present "Skepthical," a multi-agent reviewer designed to verify claims using external tools, and demonstrate its performance against other AI reviewers on astrophysics and ML preprints.

items.title: Cortex-FL: Agent-Mediated Collaboration for Federated Learning
items.abstract: Cortex-FL introduces an agent-native approach to federated learning, allowing users to specify learning goals in natural language. Its core method involves agents that automatically discover collaborators, define tasks, and manage incentives, streamlining the complex process of setting up and executing federated learning. The system's main contribution is enabling organizations without specialized expertise to easily participate in federated learning by abstracting away the coordination overhead while preserving data and computational control.
items.figure_caption: Figure 1. From (a) agentic service delegation and (b) manually coordinated FL to (c) agent-mediated FL in Cortex-FL . Three panels compare coordination workflows. Panel (a) shows an agent delegating a software task to agents, tools, and services through A2A and MCP, with x402 payments. Panel (b) shows an organizer coordinating data owners through questions about participants, learning objectives, infrastructure, and incentives. Panel (c) shows CortexFL agentic nodes on AgentaNet coordinating a classifier for cats, dogs, birds, ships, and trucks through agreements, isolated training, and incentives.

items.title: From Delegation to Coordination: Learning Efficient Multi-Agent Deep Research
items.abstract: This paper introduces LEAD-RL, a novel multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for deep research. Its core method is a joint training approach with contribution-aware credit assignment, where subagent reports are evaluated for their research utility to gate their rewards. The main contribution is improved answer quality across benchmarks by ensuring subagents provide reliable evidence, overcoming limitations of existing delegation methods.
items.figure_caption: Overview of LEAD-RL . (a) The efficient delegation harness combines dynamic task routing with local and global verification. (b) Contribution-aware RL filters team-level outcome credit using subagent report judgments and jointly updates the main agent and subagents.

The study highlights that synthetic data often outperforms human data, especially for tasks like summarization, even at substantial budget differences.

papers.title: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the multifaceted roles of decision models in long-horizon agents, moving beyond their traditional use as "actors." The core method compares decision models and LLMs as actors, judges, and teachers across ALFWorld and WebShop environments. The key contribution is demonstrating that models performing poorly as actors can still be effective teachers, and that judging actions based on their contribution to subgoals, rather than overall success, is crucial for effective learning.
papers.figure_caption: One decision model queried in three ways, on the task of putting a heated mug on a table. Actor : choosing the next action. Judge : scoring an action of a recorded trajectory under two contexts (Prefix, Hindsight) and two questions (Value, Progress). Teacher : scoring the actions of policy rollouts, with the centered scores added to the GRPO outcome advantage. The middle row lists the six models we evaluate.

papers.title: AI for Biologists: The Knowledge Boundaries of Foundation Models in the Age of Agentic Systems
papers.abstract: This paper reviews how foundation models are transforming biological research. It proposes that five key design elements define a model's "knowledge boundary," indicating the scope of reliable outputs. Understanding these boundaries is crucial for researchers and AI agents to effectively and trustworthily utilize these powerful tools.

papers.title: AURA 2.0: From User-Driven Responses to Model-Initiated Conversations in Streaming Video
papers.abstract: AURA 2.0 introduces Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC) to enable AI assistants to proactively engage users by identifying and discussing relevant events in streaming video. It also incorporates Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) for context-aware tool use and Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) for precise object referencing in both user inputs and model outputs. This moves beyond reactive AI to a more dynamic and contextually aware conversational experience.

papers.title: Ballad: Bandit-Based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Ballad, a bandit-based system for adaptively routing calls to different Large Language Models (LLMs) during automated heuristic discovery. It challenges the assumption that larger, more expensive LLMs are always better, finding their performance inconsistent. Ballad addresses the non-stationary and entangled reward signals inherent in this process to optimize LLM selection for discovering better heuristics.

papers.title: CapLite: Prompt-Injection Defense for Small Language Model Agents without Model-Written Security Artifacts
papers.abstract: This paper introduces CapLite, a novel prompt-injection defense for small language model (SLM) agents. Unlike prior methods that rely on the SLM to generate its own security artifacts, CapLite derives its policy from tool schemas and enforces write integrity by committing write calls before tool results are read and only allowing writes where all critical arguments originate from the user's request. This approach effectively prevents prompt injection attacks from manipulating agent actions.

papers.title: Compiling Known Rules into Compact Neural Agents: Weight-Space Programming on Unseen Games
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Weight-Space Programming (WSP), a method that uses language models to directly generate neural network weights, bypassing traditional training. The core contribution is demonstrating that known game mechanics can be compiled into compact neural agents that generalize to unseen game variations. The research shows that WSP can achieve high performance, even outperforming traditional NumPy players under similar computational constraints.
papers.figure_caption: Left: setup. A writer receives a game’s mechanics-only source and returns weights for the fixed actor, a network of its own design, or a Python player, one-shot (1) or with feedback (2). Learned baselines train the fixed actor on the support levels. Right: one state of the public game ls20 ( ARC Prize Foundation, 2026 ) as published and under a template we constructed for this figure. The board and HUD are turned, player, collectibles, walls and the key frame are drawn in other styles, and colours are permuted, which changes 91% of the cells while the mechanics stay the same. The private templates vary geometry, object and HUD style and palette in this way.

papers.title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
papers.abstract: CoReMem is a framework for coding agents that optimizes memory usage for successive tasks. It achieves this by valuing memory segments based on their predicted usefulness for future, unknown tasks, while also accounting for the costs of storing and accessing this memory. This allows the agent to build a compact, efficient memory and adapt its behavior to leverage it effectively.

papers.title: Designing Institutions for Autonomous AI
papers.abstract: This paper argues that designing effective "institutions" governing AI interactions is crucial for their collective capabilities and alignment, moving beyond a sole focus on individual AI models. Drawing on established social science theories, it proposes seven principles for creating AI institutions that foster cooperation, reliable judgment, and human accountability. The core contribution is establishing institutional design as a vital, distinct area of AI research.
papers.figure_caption: Institutional design as an experimental research programme. Autonomous agents operating under different institutional rules may develop different collective capabilities and patterns of alignment, even when their individual capabilities remain unchanged. Illustrated here for machine science, the same population of research agents is placed under publishing rules imported from human science or under machine-native institutional rules, producing different scientific records. Alternative institutional arrangements can then be compared using matched populations of agents. The outcome measures shown concern collective capability; collective alignment, including adherence to human-defined purposes, institutional constraints and accountability requirements, must be evaluated alongside them. Experimental comparisons can inform the subsequent revision of institutional rules.

papers.title: Discovering Effective Agent Memory Designs through Program Evolution
papers.abstract: This paper introduces MAPE, a program evolution framework that automatically discovers effective agent memory designs. MAPE iteratively diagnoses and proposes memory program improvements, leading to significant accuracy gains and cost reductions compared to manual designs. The research identifies two key design patterns: retaining raw conversations for evidence and composing retrieved evidence based on query intent, which are shown to improve performance when transplanted into existing memory systems.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of MAPE ’s program evolution framework. Candidate programs are proposed using archived designs and diagnostic feedback, checked for execution errors, and evaluated on the search set. Their implementations, results, and diagnoses are retained to guide subsequent proposals. Evolution follows either an accuracy-only objective ( MAPE-A ) or joint accuracy–cost objectives ( MAPE-P ). Shortlisted programs undergo held-out evaluation for final selection.

papers.title: Reasoning Supervision and Capability Retention in LoRA Domain Adaptation
papers.abstract: This paper investigates LoRA domain adaptation for financial tasks, aiming to improve performance without sacrificing generalization. The core method involves comparing three LoRA training regimes: response-only, single-adapter reasoning (including teacher model traces), and dual-adapter composite training. The contribution is demonstrating that response-only LoRA effectively boosts in-domain performance, particularly calibration and accuracy, while largely preserving the model's general capabilities.

papers.title: Skill Adapter: Personalized Modification and Online Routing of General-Purpose Skills
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Skill Adapter, a method for personalizing and dynamically routing general-purpose skills for LLM agents. It achieves this by learning local adjustments from user feedback and storing them as "Adapters" linked to core skills. A routing agent then selects the most relevant skills and Adapters based on the current task context, enabling efficient and personalized skill utilization.
papers.figure_caption: The influence of user requirements on skill selection and composition. In contract translation, layout-preservation requirements affect document extraction and make layout reconstruction part of the subsequent workflow. Task descriptions and user feedback jointly inform skill adjustments and the selection of execution procedures.

papers.title: The Value of Thinking: Learning When to Reason in Hybrid Decision Models
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a "zero-or-$T$ thinking" paradigm for hybrid decision models. Instead of deciding how much to reason, a model either answers directly (zero thinking) or performs full autoregressive reasoning ($T$ tokens). A self-routing block estimates the "value of thinking" and triggers full reasoning only when its expected utility exceeds a cost threshold, optimizing for efficiency in agentic tasks.
papers.figure_caption: HDM’s zero-or- T T thinking on two JevBench questions. LEFT, a case where the fast mode is sufficient: the predicted value of thinking is below \( \lambda \) , the block answers at no token, and running both modes afterwards confirms the slow mode would not have changed the answer. RIGHT, a case that should go to the slow mode: the predicted value is above \( \lambda \) , routing to the slow mode, and running both modes afterwards confirms the fast answer would have been wrong. Appendix G gives both thinking blocks in full.

papers.title: AnalogLayoutWorld: An Open Benchmark for Agentic Analog Layout Design
papers.abstract: This paper introduces **AnalogLayoutWorld**, an open benchmark designed to evaluate the capabilities of AI agents in analog circuit layout design. The benchmark provides a realistic environment with expert-reviewed tasks, integrated design tools, and comprehensive verification, addressing the challenges of long-horizon engineering tasks with physical constraints. Its core contribution is establishing a standardized platform for developing and assessing agents in this complex domain, revealing current agent performance and highlighting areas for improvement.
papers.figure_caption: Agentic analog layout design process. (a) A fixed netlist, specifications, and process design kit define the task. (b) The agent constructs and refines layouts using layout tools and verification feedback. (c) Integration, fabrication, and silicon characterization provide physical validation.

papers.title: Auditing AI peer reviewers: a benchmark on real scientific papers
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a benchmark for evaluating AI peer reviewers by injecting specific, localized errors into real scientific papers. The benchmark measures reviewers' ability to detect these errors across different types and severities, alongside their false-positive rates. The authors also present "Skepthical," a multi-agent reviewer designed to verify claims using external tools, and demonstrate its performance against other AI reviewers on astrophysics and ML preprints.

papers.title: Cortex-FL: Agent-Mediated Collaboration for Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Cortex-FL introduces an agent-native approach to federated learning, allowing users to specify learning goals in natural language. Its core method involves agents that automatically discover collaborators, define tasks, and manage incentives, streamlining the complex process of setting up and executing federated learning. The system's main contribution is enabling organizations without specialized expertise to easily participate in federated learning by abstracting away the coordination overhead while preserving data and computational control.
papers.figure_caption: Figure 1. From (a) agentic service delegation and (b) manually coordinated FL to (c) agent-mediated FL in Cortex-FL . Three panels compare coordination workflows. Panel (a) shows an agent delegating a software task to agents, tools, and services through A2A and MCP, with x402 payments. Panel (b) shows an organizer coordinating data owners through questions about participants, learning objectives, infrastructure, and incentives. Panel (c) shows CortexFL agentic nodes on AgentaNet coordinating a classifier for cats, dogs, birds, ships, and trucks through agreements, isolated training, and incentives.

papers.title: From Delegation to Coordination: Learning Efficient Multi-Agent Deep Research
papers.abstract: This paper introduces LEAD-RL, a novel multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for deep research. Its core method is a joint training approach with contribution-aware credit assignment, where subagent reports are evaluated for their research utility to gate their rewards. The main contribution is improved answer quality across benchmarks by ensuring subagents provide reliable evidence, overcoming limitations of existing delegation methods.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of LEAD-RL . (a) The efficient delegation harness combines dynamic task routing with local and global verification. (b) Contribution-aware RL filters team-level outcome credit using subagent report judgments and jointly updates the main agent and subagents.
